title: Ezekiel 6:1–14
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel, telling him to prophesy to the mountains of Israel, the hills, watercourses, and valleys where high places and altars to idols stood (6:1–7). The LORD will bring a sword on these places, breaking altars and idols; the language echoes Leviticus 26:30. Then comes a turn: “Yet I will leave a remnant” (6:8). Those who escape will remember the LORD among the nations, recognize how their heart turned from him, and loathe their own evil (6:8–10). Jeremiah’s repeated word that the LORD will not make “a full end” (Jeremiah 4:27; 5:10, 18; 30:11) is a related remnant theme, named here without harmonizing. The prophet is then told to clap and stamp in lament (6:11–14). The recurring refrain “you will know that I am the LORD” runs through the chapter. On the heart and its turning (6:9), see the existing keyContrast at Deuteronomy 10:16 rather than a new one.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s message continues to come from God, step by step, rather than from his own reflection on events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as marking a new oracle grounded in divine authority. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a fresh message, now directed to the land itself rather than to the city.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy to them,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel is to set his face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy to them. Arminian readers see the mountains addressed because they were sites of idolatrous worship, where the people had turned from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that addressing the land personifies it as a witness to Israel’s sin. Both traditions read setting the face as resolute prophetic opposition, aimed at the places where false worship flourished.

verses.text: and say, ‘You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! The Lord GOD says to the mountains and to the hills, to the watercourses and to the valleys: “Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword on you, and I will destroy your high places.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD tells the mountains, hills, watercourses, and valleys that he will bring a sword and destroy the high places. Arminian readers see every corner of the landscape implicated in idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Leviticus 26:30 by reference, where the LORD warned he would destroy high places. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as judgment on false worship sites, fulfilling long-standing covenant warnings.

verses.text: Your altars will become desolate, and your incense altars will be broken. I will cast down your slain men before your idols.
verses.arminianNotes: Altars will be desolate and incense altars broken, and the slain will be cast down before idols. Arminian readers see a grim irony: the worshipers fall before the very idols that cannot save them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the judgment matching the sin, with idolatry’s sites becoming places of death. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as exposing the powerlessness of idols, without elaborating the violence.

verses.text: I will lay the dead bodies of the children of Israel before their idols. I will scatter your bones around your altars.
verses.arminianNotes: Dead bodies will lie before idols, and bones will be scattered around altars. Arminian readers note that this defiles the sites, ending their use for worship and showing their emptiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as the final dishonor of idolatrous worship. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stark covenant judgment, compare Leviticus 26:30, and they handle its imagery briefly and soberly.

verses.text: In all your dwelling places, the cities will be laid waste and the high places will be desolate, so that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your incense altars may be cut down, and your works may be abolished.
verses.arminianNotes: Cities will be laid waste and high places desolate, so that altars, idols, and incense altars are broken and abolished. Arminian readers see God clearing the land of the objects that had drawn the people away from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the purpose clauses showing that the destruction aims at ending idolatry. Both traditions read the verse as purposeful judgment: the LORD removes false worship so that his people might know him.

verses.text: The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The slain will fall, and you will know that I am the LORD. Arminian readers see the refrain as God’s desire to be known, even through judgment, which can open eyes that warnings did not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the recognition formula as central to Ezekiel’s theology, appearing throughout the book. Shared ground: both traditions read knowing the LORD as the goal of these oracles, reached here through sober judgment.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Yet I will leave a remnant, in that you will have some that escape the sword among the nations, when you are scattered through the countries.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, Yet I will leave a remnant, some escaping the sword among the nations. Arminian readers see mercy within judgment, a turn that shows God’s purposes are not only destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign preservation of a remnant, a theme related to Jeremiah’s word that the LORD will not make a full end (Jeremiah 4:27; 30:11 by reference). Both traditions name the parallel without harmonizing the two prophets’ wording.

verses.text: Those of you that escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken with their lewd heart, which has departed from me, and with their eyes, which play the prostitute after their idols. Then they will loathe themselves in their own sight for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who escape will remember the LORD, see how their heart departed, and loathe their evils. Arminian readers see genuine repentance arising as the exiles reflect on their unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working repentance through judgment, compare Ezekiel 11:19 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heartfelt remembrance; on God’s work and human response in the heart, see the existing keyContrast at Deuteronomy 10:16.

verses.text: They will know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: They will know that the LORD did not speak in vain about the evil he would bring. Arminian readers see the exiles coming to recognize that God’s warnings were real and his word trustworthy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of God’s word as vindicating his truthfulness. Both traditions read the verse as showing that judgment confirms the reliability of what the LORD has spoken, and that this recognition is part of the remnant’s restoration.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says: ‘Strike with your hand, and stamp with your foot, and say, “Alas!”, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel; for they will fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD tells Ezekiel to clap, stamp, and cry Alas over Israel’s abominations, for sword, famine, and pestilence are coming. Arminian readers see the prophet’s gestures as lament, grieving the coming disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some read the gestures as grief and others as emphasis or even scorn toward the sin; the text says Alas. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an emotionally charged sign, focused on the evil that brings judgment.

verses.text: He who is far off will die of the pestilence. He who is near will fall by the sword. He who remains and is besieged will die by the famine. Thus I will accomplish my wrath on them.
verses.arminianNotes: The far off die by pestilence, the near by sword, and those besieged by famine, as the LORD accomplishes his wrath. Arminian readers see no place of escape for those who persist in rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comprehensive reach of the judgment, covering every location. Both traditions read the verse as stressing that distance or nearness cannot shield anyone from the consequences the LORD has announced.

verses.text: You will know that I am the LORD when their slain men are among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the tops of the mountains, under every green tree, and under every thick oak—the places where they offered pleasant aroma to all their idols.
verses.arminianNotes: They will know the LORD when the slain lie among idols on every high hill and under every green tree. Arminian readers note the list of worship sites, recalling Deuteronomy 12:2 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the places of false worship turned into places of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking the scene of sin with the scene of consequence, so that the LORD is known through it.

verses.text: I will stretch out my hand on them and make the land desolate and waste, from the wilderness toward Diblah, throughout all their habitations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will stretch out his hand and make the land desolate from the wilderness toward Diblah. Arminian readers note that the place named is uncertain, and that the sense is clearly the whole land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outstretched hand as the LORD’s power in judgment. Both traditions read the verse as covering the land from one extent to another, closing with the refrain that they will know that he is the LORD.
